summary:
Poltergeist is an interactive coastal observatory, providing insight into what you can learn about a changing coast with different satellites. Built for the "Dancing with the SARs" project, it combines data from NASA-ISRO NISAR, Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2, ground-based LiDAR surveys, and environmental measurements from Duck, North Carolina.

We created an interactive, map-based tool, that includes 2D and 3D terrain, survey comparisons, beach profiles, and transparent scientific validation. It calculates changes in ground elevation from LiDAR, uses physics-based tide correction to validate optical waterlines, and assesses whether NISAR enhances satellite estimates of change in elevation.

Consistent with other EO instruments, Poltergeist is likely to reveal inconsistencies because sensors detect different physical features in different ways. This tool shows acquisition times, sensor signal uncertainty and model limitations and enables users to tell how much of what they see is real and how much is caused by satellite artifacts. The product provides reliable evidence crucial for erosion monitoring and future planning of the coast.
details:
When satellites detect coastal change, how do we know what's actually happening on the ground?

The Problem

Satellites are powerful tools for monitoring coastal erosion, but their measurements can be misleading. Changes in tides, waves, vegetation, and surface conditions can make a coastline appear different even when the land itself hasn't changed.

A 2026 study by Mikkelsen et al., published in Scientific Reports, found that satellite-derived shorelines do not always correspond to the same physical coastal feature. Another 2026 study by Aladejana et al. highlighted how tidal, wave, and measurement uncertainties can make apparent shoreline changes difficult to interpret.

These findings reveal the problem we're addressing: satellites can detect change, but interpreting that change accurately is much harder.

Our Solution

POLTERGEIST is an interactive coastal observatory that helps users explore satellite observations and verify what they actually mean.

Our solution utilizes a mult-sensor based approach from different datasets from different sources: NISAR, Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, and USACE LiDAR

Our platform allows users to explore satellite layers, compare observations across dates, examine radar changes, visualize coastal elevation differences, and investigate scientific findings through an interactive 2D/3D map.

Instead of simply showing where satellite images differ, POLTERGEIST helps users understand why they differ and whether the available evidence supports physical coastal change.

Our Results

49.7% reduction in shoreline-position RMSE (7.42 m → 3.73 m) through tide correction.

50.4% RMSE reduction in a separate validation benchmark.

26.8 cm median beach lowering measured across 17,654 cells.

11,684 m² of coastal terrain experienced measurable lowering greater than 10 cm.

45% disagreement between NISAR and Sentinel-1 radar-scattering changes.

Technology and Creativity

We developed POLTERGEIST using Python, FastAPI, React, JavaScript/TypeScript, and MapLibre, integrating data from NASA Earthdata, Copernicus, USACE, and NOAA.

What makes POLTERGEIST different is its interactive, evidence-first approach. Users can investigate NISAR radar changes, compare multiple observation systems, examine real elevation measurements, and explore how correcting for tides changes shoreline estimates.

Rather than hiding uncertainty, the platform helps users see where satellite measurements agree, disagree, or remain inconclusive.

Intended Impact

POLTERGEIST makes complex coastal satellite data easier to explore and understand. It could support coastal researchers, environmental educators, and future monitoring initiatives by making satellite observations more transparent and interpretable.

Our current demonstration focuses on Duck, North Carolina. Future development could extend the system to additional coastlines and longer NISAR observation histories.

Our mission: Don't just detect change. Understand it. Verify it.

Research References

  1. Mikkelsen et al. (2026). Resolving uncertainty in satellite-derived shorelines of a reef-lined beach using high spatiotemporal resolution topographic surveys. Scientific Reports. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-026-54336-z
  2. Aladejana et al. (2026). When is satellite-derived shoreline change interpretable? A signal-to-noise framework for shoreline-change detectability. Regional Studies in Marine Science. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.rsma.2026.105374
